Iran says three tankers hit mines in Hormuz despite U.S. escort
Iranian forces said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. widened sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel.
Washington is reportedly investigating Iran as a primary suspect behind dozens of cyberattacks on energy tankers: WSJ.
MUSCAT, OMAN - NOVEMBER 19: A view of the commercial ships and oil tankers waiting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the most important strategic waterways for global trade, seen from the Gulf of Oman on November 19, 2026.
Iranian forces said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest in a string of incidents in the waterway, as the U.S. escalates sanctions aimed at cutting off Tehran's financial lifelines.
In a statement carried by state news agency IRNA, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three "offending" oil tankers "suffered a severe explosion and fire after hitting naval mines" in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Guards said one tanker was near the southern coast and two were in the eastern part of the strait. All three were under extensive U.S. military air cover and escort that failed to prevent the explosions.
"U.S. military cover and escort will not replace compliance with maritime regulations and instructions from the IRGC Navy Traffic Control Center," the statement said.
Iranian forces have repeatedly warned commercial vessels that only the northern shipping lane has been approved by Tehran for safe passage, while attacking or threatening ships that use alternative routes near Oman.
The U.S. added a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, to the Gulf last week, joining two other carriers in the fleet enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The tanker incidents came after the U.S. Treasury on Monday announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key personnel as part of what it called "a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks."
Iran's economy has come under growing pressure as Washington expanded sanctions under its so-called "Operation Economic Outcast" since August, aimed at crippling financial networks behind the country's oil revenue.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in Monday's statement, described Iran's economy as "underwater," saying its shadow banking system was "the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime."
President Trump is 'stuck', has not learned much from the Iran war: Analyst
The conflict also appears to have extended to cyberspace, with Washington investigating Iran as a primary suspect behind dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers, The Wall Street Journal reported Monday .
As many as 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals and other potentially hazardous cargoes were believed to have been targeted, while some received warnings and bomb threats, the Journal reported, citing U.S. officials and others familiar with the matter.
U.S. authorities were also examining Russia as another possible culprit, according to the report, which described the widening attacks and occasional ransom messages as part of Iran's efforts to stoke fear among shipowners and further disrupt energy flows.
The foreign ministries of Iran and Russia did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
The conflict, triggered by the U.S. and Israeli strikes in late February, has seen Tehran close the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. impose a blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf, squeezing energy shipments through one of the world's most critical shipping conduits.
Oil futures inched lower Tuesday as investors looked past continued attacks on tankers to price in rising supplies from the region. On Tuesday, international benchmark Brent futures dipped to $89.2 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude fell to $80.1 per barrel, down from the October high of nearly $105 per barrel.
Pressure on oil prices has eased as regional crude supply recovered and Russian exports rebounded, loosening supply constraints ahead of winter, said Gregory Brew, senior analyst for Iran and energy at Eurasia Group.
Russian refined-product exports recovered in November, with diesel shipments rising back to 400,000 barrels per day, Brew said. But "intensifying Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz could reverse that trend," he added, estimating Brent would remain in the lower half of an $80-100-per-barrel range.

Fact-check: Is more oil going through the Strait of Hormuz than before the Iran war?
“The insurance costs of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have gone up substantially, even though there’s more oil going through the strait today than there was pre-war," Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds said in a Nov. 8 interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press."

Even though Florida defied midterm trends to maintain Republican control, its incoming governor acknowledged that voters hit a breaking point over high living costs.
In a Nov. 8 interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press ,” host Kristen Welker played Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds a clip of the state’s current Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, criticizing GOP candidates who blamed high gas prices on former President Joe Biden, instead of the Iran war.
“I didn’t really hear any Republicans trying to blame gas prices today on what the Biden team was doing,” he said, pivoting to oil shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
“I actually just read an article from The Wall Street Journal about this,” he said. “The insurance costs of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have gone up substantially, even though there’s more oil going through the strait today than there was pre-war.”
That’s misleading, and omits key context about oil flow in the region.
Donalds did not respond to PolitiFact’s request for more information. But he referenced The Wall Street Journal, which published an Oct. 20 story headlined, “More oil is now coming out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran war.”
The article describes a single week in October during which more oil was transported through the Persian Gulf — which includes, but is not limited to, the Strait of Hormuz — compared with pre-war levels of about 23 million barrels per day, according to ship tracker Kpler.
It’s important to note that the region’s oil flows fluctuate, and different tracking organizations arrive at varying figures. And, as The Wall Street Journal story also notes, the average amount of oil passing through the strait itself remains below pre-war levels, refuting Donalds’ statement.
Skip York, an energy and global oil fellow at Rice University’s Center for Energy Studies, said there were several days in October when oil moving through the Gulf region reached over 20 million barrels per day, but the flow isn’t exceeding pre-conflict levels.
That traffic doesn’t mean the U.S.-Iran conflict is winding down or that operations in the strait have returned to normal, experts said. Instead, it’s driven by money: Oil traders and ship operators stand to profit massively if they are able to get oil through the strait to sell to international markets.
“What makes this remarkable is that we have seen increasing traffic through Hormuz even though the middle of the month saw a dramatic ramp-up of attempted Iranian interdictions (drone and missile attacks),” York said in an email. “In fact, about half of the vessels hit since the conflict started in March happened in the month of October.”
More oil is moving through Hormuz since war began, but below pre-war levels
During the week ending Oct. 18, The Wall Street Journal reported that overall Middle East oil flows, including shipments through Hormuz and alternative routes across the region, averaged more than 24 million barrels a day, surpassing pre-war levels of 23.3 million barrels a day, according to ship tracker Kpler.
The story says preliminary figures show Hormuz oil flows, including offshore transfers in the Gulf of Oman, “came to around 14 million barrels a day on average for the same period, or 82% of pre-war levels.”
Other data show that Strait of Hormuz traffic has remained below pre-war levels.
Vortexa, a data analytics company for global energy and freight markets, looked at all Middle East oil flows, which includes flows through the strait and exports from Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, the United Arab Emirates and Oman’s ports outside of the strait. For the same week ending Oct. 18, Vortexa found those flows reached 19.2 million barrels a day. That’s below the 24 million barrels that Journal cited, but marks some of the highest oil flows through the Persian Gulf since the war began.
The following week, Vortexa estimated that 15.1 million barrels of oil made it through the Gulf region per day, and 17.1 million barrels per day the week after that. In the Strait of Hormuz alone, the organization found that  9.2 million barrels of oil made it through each day in the week ending Oct. 18.
Reuters reported Nov. 3 that Gulf oil exports dipped in October from September, when exports were the ‌highest since the war started.
Vortexa found Middle East flows of crude and refined oil products averaged around 17.1 million barrels per day in October, according to Reuters, a drop from ‌18.9 million barrels per day in September.  The figures could be revised upward slightly as tankers have ramped up efforts to avoid detection, and could be missing from official estimates.
Tanker Trackers, a maritime intelligence company that tracks oil shipments found that overall Middle East crude oil exports averaged around 18.7 million barrels per day in the week ending Nov. 5. During that time, the organization said 13.1 million barrels went through Hormuz,  below pre-war levels.
Increased tanker traffic through the strait has to do with profit, not security
Heightened wartime oil traffic in the region shows charterers and boat operators are willing to take safety risks for big payouts.
“It’s the exact opposite of a success story,” said Clark Williams-Derry, an energy finance analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, who also pointed to attacks on ships traversing the strait hitting an all-time high in October . Any recovery in oil flows happened in spite of the volatile maritime environment, he said.
Some Gulf states, such as Saudi Arabia and Iraq, dropped the asking price for oil in order to lure back buyers who had been scared off by the war’s shipping risks in the strait or nearby waterways.
To capture profits from shipping oil from the Gulf to much higher-priced international markets, charterers (such as national oil companies that hire ships or tankers to transport oil) are paying astronomical daily freight rates of around $1 million a day , energy experts said.
“If you can move a million barrels of oil through the Strait, you can make tens of millions of dollars on a short-ish trip to Asia. Worth it to find a vessel that’s willing to take the risk,” Williams-Derry said.
The situation remains precarious. Movement through the strait could stall if fighting resumes and the expensive operation contributes to ongoing high prices at the pump.
Donalds said, “There’s more oil going through the Strait (of Hormuz) today than there was pre-war.”
In recent weeks, daily oil flows through the Persian Gulf region, which includes the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, have occasionally matched or exceeded pre-war levels, but it isn’t happening consistently.
The average amount of oil passing through the strait itself remains below pre-war levels.
Oil flows through the region, and the strait, remain lower than before the war began.
Gulf shipping routes are still dangerous, with tankers braving them for big payouts, not because of improved security.
Donalds’ statement contains an element of truth — regional oil flows have occasionally surpassed prewar levels — but it misleads in that wartime flows through the strait itself are lower than they were before the war. We rate it Mostly False.
PolitiFact Chief Correspondent Louis Jacobson contributed to this report.

items.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
items.summary: German media said Russia planned to launch a satellite with a nuclear warhead into space in coming weeks.
items.content:
Image caption, Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said such reports were "not new, yet they remain no less shocking", and a government spokesman said the reports were being taken "very seriously".
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports but dismissed stories citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper SÃ¼ddeutscher Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.
Asked about the reports, the Nato secretary general told a press conference in Berlin alongside Merz: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
The Western defensive alliance had a variety of response options, said Rutte.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary."
Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, told the Handeslblatt newspaper that having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario".
Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit.
Bleddyn Bowen, co-director of the Space Research Centre at Durham University, said that exploding a nuclear weapon in space would have "massive infrastructural effects" as there were now more than 15,000 active satellites. But he told the BBC's Today programme that "the effect of these weapons would be extremely indiscriminate and also take out a lot of Russia's own space infrastructure".
Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US accused Russia of developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation .
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.
In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

items.content:
Figure caption, A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Image caption, Trunmp and Xi ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen last week
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.
The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.
Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.
Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.
The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.
Image caption, Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in Berlin in October
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.
He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.
If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

items.content:
US Stock Futures Mixed After Nvidia-Led Rally as Investors Assess Federal Reserve Rate Outlook: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
US stock futures traded mixed on Tuesday following a sharp rally on Wall Street, as investors assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's reinstatement as chief executive of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and the outlook for Federal Reserve interest rates.
Asian equity markets also recorded substantial gains, particularly in Taiwan and South Korea, although concerns surrounding artificial intelligence investment and financing costs remained.
Nvidia Shares Retreat in Premarket Trading Following Monday's Rally
Nvidia shares declined by more than 3% in premarket trading on Tuesday after gaining more than 30% during Monday's session, adding over US$1 trillion to the company's market capitalisation.
The rally followed Huang's reinstatement as chief executive, approximately two weeks after his resignation.
The announcement supported a broader recovery across US equity markets, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 6.51%, the S&P 500 advancing 4.73% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rising 3.01%.
It marked the strongest session for US equity markets since April 2025.
"Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO lifted stocks on Monday and cleared the negative sentiment, opening room for a near-term rebound," analysts at BCA Research said in a research note.
The recovery extended into Asian markets, with Taiwanese equities rising 8.99% and South Korea's KOSPI index advancing 6.32%.
Both markets are home to major semiconductor manufacturers supplying components used in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Under Huang's leadership, Nvidia has expanded from its traditional gaming semiconductor business into a major supplier of advanced processors used in AI datacentres.
The company has also invested in businesses operating across the AI sector, including financing arrangements involving some of its customers.
However, questions remain regarding the financial returns from substantial AI infrastructure expenditure and the sustainability of investment supported by debt financing.
Huang is also expected to appear before US congressional committees, where Nvidia's commercial relationships with China and compliance with semiconductor export restrictions could face further scrutiny.
Federal Reserve's John Williams Comments on Inflation Outlook
Investors continue to anticipate a further Federal Reserve interest rate increase in December, following October's 25-basis-point rise, the central bank's first increase since 2023.
Minutes from the October meeting indicated that most policymakers considered another rate increase necessary to address inflationary pressures, partly associated with higher energy prices resulting from the conflict involving Iran.
One Federal Reserve governor has suggested that a larger increase of 50 basis points could be appropriate.
However, New York Federal Reserve President John Williams offered a more moderate assessment of inflationary pressures following Monday's market close.
Williams indicated that inflation associated with tariffs had largely subsided and that housing services inflation had slowed.
"Inflation expectations remain well anchored," Williams argued, adding that he expects price growth to slow to just above the Fed's 2% target level in 2027.
Higher borrowing costs remain a potential concern for companies financing AI infrastructure development through debt.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise Shares Fall Despite Results Exceeding Expectations
Hewlett Packard Enterprise (NYSE:HPE) shares declined by more than 9% in premarket trading on Tuesday, following a gain of more than 17% during Monday's broader market rally.
The technology company reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of US$14.55 billion and free cash flow of US$1.92 billion, both exceeding consensus estimates cited by CNBC.
According to analysts at Vital Knowledge, the results were supported by HPE's cloud and artificial intelligence division, where sales increased by approximately 69% and orders more than doubled.
HPE expects adjusted earnings per share of between US$1.30 and US$1.40 for the current quarter, with revenue forecast at between US$14 billion and US$14.6 billion.
Both forecasts exceeded Wall Street expectations, as did the company's fiscal 2027 earnings and revenue projections.
HPE also announced an additional US$5 billion share buyback.
Despite the stronger-than-expected results, analysts at Vital Knowledge highlighted uncertainty surrounding longer-term AI infrastructure expenditure, particularly between 2027 and 2029, as additional manufacturing capacity becomes available.
Brent Crude Trades Below US$90 Amid Supply Surplus Expectations
Oil prices extended recent declines as expectations of excess global supply outweighed concerns surrounding continued tensions in the Middle East.
Brent crude traded at approximately US$88 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures stood at around US$79 per barrel.
The International Energy Agency recently forecast a global oil supply surplus of two million barrels per day during the fourth quarter of 2026, citing a recovery in Gulf exports.
Middle Eastern oil producers have been pursuing alternative export routes to address regional supply disruptions, while the US military has provided security for some vessels travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.
Goldman Sachs recently forecast that continued progress in restoring export flows could contribute to a substantial global oil supply surplus in 2027.

Iran has reiterated that it will use “ all available means ” to confront the United States naval blockade, as it has stepped up attacks on tankers attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, signalling potential escalation.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that they would “definitely not tolerate” the naval blockade, and would use “all our tools to confront this US aggression”.

“Iran has the right to use any available tool to defend itself in this regard,” he said.
The naval blockade has largely halted Iranian oil exports. It was first imposed in April, but was lifted following the June memorandum of understanding. The blockade was reinstated weeks later after the agreement collapsed.
As Iran’s economy is increasingly squeezed by the US-led economic sanctions, attacks on tankers have also gone up, affecting the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. The disruption to the flow of oil has triggered a global energy crisis.
What do we know about the attacks on tankers, and how frequent are they?
Attacks on oil tankers and commercial vessels have continued throughout the war, but more recently, a rising number of tankers have erupted in flames after hitting naval mines purportedly placed by Iran. More than 25 tankers have been hit in the past week alone.
According to reports, tankers have continued to make the dangerous journey through the waterway without seeking Iran’s approval, often travelling in the dark and without navigation transponders to avoid alerting Iranian officials.
However, this clandestine approach has come with its own problems.
On Tuesday morning, Iran’s navy said two oil tankers had hit mines and caught fire in the waterway, according to a statement reported by Iran’s Tasnim news agency.
According to the statement, the tankers entered a restricted zone east of the strait after turning off their navigation and identification systems.
The statement reiterated that the strait would not be opened until Iran’s objectives and demands were met, including halting hostilities, lifting the blockade and waiving sanctions, adding that “owners of oil tankers are required to coordinate with the armed forces to ensure safe passage through this strategic strait.”
At the same time, the commander of the Iranian army, Amir Hatami, called for tightening the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, stressing that Tehran needed to make conditions more difficult.
“We must tighten our control over the Strait of Hormuz, our management of it must be stronger, and conditions must become more difficult for the enemy,” Iranian television quoted Hatami as saying, during a speech to senior army commanders at the Command and Staff University.
The head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) navy, Ali Ozmaei, also warned vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz against using unapproved shipping routes.
“The Strait of Hormuz is not a place to test unauthorised routes and ignore maritime warnings,” Ozmaei said, according to the ISNA news agency.
Despite the attacks, oil prices have fallen, with Brent crude futures at $88.35 per barrel as supplies recover . At one point, oil prices went past $120 per barrel.
So far, according to the AIS ship-tracking platform, in the past 24 hours, 28 ships have crossed the strait: 12 into the Gulf and 16 out of it, carrying an estimated 4.18 million barrels of oil.
However, because it only collects data from vessels with transponders on, loopholes – including the no-signal bypass routes – mean it is not an accurate count of how many ships are crossing the strait.
Still, it is a huge drop from pre-war numbers, during which 125 to 140 ships used to pass through daily.
In the past week, Iran has also carried out attacks on US bases in the Gulf, targeting radars.
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Iran had launched “more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year”, adding that they had all been downed and had caused no damage.
Meanwhile, last week, US Central Command ( CENTCOM ) said in an advisory that ships receiving cargo from vessels loaded at Iranian ports or along the country’s coastline could be considered to be “evading the blockade”, which had allowed some Iranian petroleum products to reach international markets.
But Iran has repeatedly warned against US efforts to hamper its trade.
According to data from Marine Traffic, a ship-tracking platform, the number of vessels crossing between November 1 and 23 has dropped as the month goes on.
In the first week of November, between the 1st and 7th, 226 vessels entered or exited the Gulf. In the last week of the month, from the 17th to the 23rd, only 125 vessels crossed the waterway. That’s a drop of more than 40 percent.
Throughout the month, the highest day with 29 vessels exiting took place on November 1, and the highest day entering the Gulf was November 7.
In contrast, the lowest day for exiting the Gulf was on Sunday, when only one vessel left the waterway; on the same day, only two vessels entered the waterway, the lowest figure for the month.

Ukraine war: Russia warns NATO member Estonia of ‘open war’
Russia accused Estonia of “hostile actions” and warned its border measures risk open war, as Tallinn prepares to close road crossings from Dec. 1.
Estonia rejected Moscow’s claims, saying Russia was trying to deflect attention from its own actions against European security.
Recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets have raised concern about spillover risks, while analysts say a near-term peace deal remains unlikely.
The Narva Castle (R) and the Ivangorod Fortress (L) are pictured and the border bridge across the Narva River in Narva, on January 15, 2026.
Russia's Foreign Ministry has lashed out at Estonia's government, accusing the NATO member of carrying out a range of "hostile actions" and putting the Baltic state "on the verge of unleashing open war" with Moscow.
The outburst underscores rising tensions between Russia and countries on NATO's eastern flank and comes after Estonia announced it will close its road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1.
Russia's ministry said Monday it had lodged a formal protest to Estonia's chargé d'affaires, Marek Uhtegi, over Tallinn's decision to close its border crossings and accused the European Union member of imposing a naval blockade against Moscow.
"The Estonian diplomat was again informed that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of unleashing open war with Russia," the ministry said in a statement, describing measures taken by Estonian lawmakers as "Russophobic."
The ministry also accused Estonia of "tacitly" providing its airspace for Ukrainian drone flights and sharply criticized Tallinn's ban on the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain through Estonian territory, referring to a policy that was introduced at the start of October.
Estonia, which shares a 294-kilometer (183-mile) border with Russia, swiftly denied ever allowing its territory to be used for military operations by another country.
It also responded to Russia's allegations by saying the Kremlin appears to be seeking to divert attention from its own efforts to undermine European security.
"Russian missiles have reached Polish territory, Danish security services have identified an assassination plot in Denmark orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, merchant vessels in the Black Sea are under constant threat from Russian attacks, and in Estonia, an arson attack targeting a defence industry company, planned on the orders of Russian military intelligence, was foiled," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Monday.
"All this is happening while Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine," he added.
In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow on November 6, 2026.
The rhetoric marks a significant escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia. Tallinn, a staunch Ukraine ally, has frequently raised the alarm over sabotage attacks against NATO countries that have been supporting Kyiv since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
Earlier this month, Estonia said it would close road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1 as it blames Moscow for an attempted "sabotage" of one of its defense companies, an allegation the Kremlin denies.
Tallinn has said the border closure will help to reduce Moscow's ability to conduct hostile activities against it and mitigate risks related to sanctions circumvention.
Ukraine has stepped up its attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Russian President Vladimir Putin 's prized Crimea bridge , striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port .
The suspected Ukrainian attack on a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday prompted Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the Ukraine war is "spilling over" into its immediate vicinity.
Finland, one of NATO's newest members , has also closed its land border crossings with Russia.
Russia the 'biggest winner' in trilateral talks: Control Risks
Ukraine's latest attacks on some of Russia's most protected targets have demonstrated Kyiv's capabilities to hurt Moscow even without ample U.S. military support, according to Mario Bikarski, senior Europe and Central Asia analyst for Verisk Maplecroft, a political risk consultancy.
"Ukraine will continue to look for ways to degrade not only Russia's economy, but also its geostrategic interests in the wider region, including the Mediterranean and the Middle East," Bikarski said.
The prospect of an imminent peace deal between Russia and Ukraine appears to be slim, Bikarski said, although "the latest surge in diplomatic activity and mounting losses for both sides signals an appetite from all sides to reach an agreement."

Treasury yields steady after inflation warning from Fed's Williams
NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 23: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) on November 23, 2026 in New York City.
U.S. Treasury yields inched lower on Tuesday as investors took stock of a speech by John Williams of the New York Fed and looked ahead to a 5-year bond auction due later in the session.
The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, student loans and credit card debt — was down more than 2 basis points at 4.896%.
The 2-year Treasury note yield , the most sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was lower by more than 1 basis point at 4.648%. The 30-year Treasury yield — which often reacts the most to geopolitical developments — was also down more than 1 basis point at 5.279%
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Monetary policy will need to adjust to "get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis," Williams, president and chief executive of the New York Fed, said on Monday.
"There is still work to do to get that done," Williams added in comments at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York.
He said the latest economic data shows "the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high."
William's comments come ahead of the December FOMC meeting on 8-9 December. Investors are now pricing in a 100% chance of another interest rate hike, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, with a 25 basis point increase expected.
Later on Tuesday, investors will be watching a $70 billion 5-year Treasury auction as the latest supply test, as well as the consumer confidence print for November. The October reading of the personal consumption expenditures price index, which measures underlying inflation, is due Wednesday. A rise of 0.3% is expected, according to economists polled by Dow Jones.
Revised GDP data, also due on Wednesday, is expected to confirm that the U.S. economy expanded by 3.4% in the third quarter, according to Trading Economics forecasts. This compares to 2.2% growth in the second quarter.

(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot  gold prices were modestly lower and  silver prices were sharply lower in early U.S. trading Tuesday, as a firm U.S. dollar and expectations for additional Federal Reserve interest rate increases continued to pressure precious metals ahead of key inflation figures. Gold struggled to extend Monday's recovery from a 14-month low, while silver gave back part of its recent rebound amid concerns about industrial demand and restrictive monetary policy. Renewed tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz provided limited support to bullion as investors remained focused on the outlook for interest rates. At approximately 8:37 a.m. EST, spot gold was trading near $3,621.70 an ounce, down $12.50, or 0.34%, while silver was trading near $42.040 an ounce, down $1.000, or 2.33%, on the session. Gold had traded between $3,606.80 and $3,679.00 during the day, while silver's range extended from $41.710 to $44.080.
Monday's U.S. economic data indicated that business activity continued expanding in November, although growth moderated as elevated prices and tighter financial conditions constrained demand. The preliminary S&P Global U.S. composite purchasing managers' index declined to 54.6 from 55.9 in October, its lowest reading since July. The manufacturing PMI eased to 54.5 from 54.9, while the services PMI declined to 54.7 from 56.1, falling below expectations for a reading near 55.5. New orders continued increasing but at their slowest pace in four months, while employment growth remained relatively firm as companies worked to reduce outstanding orders. Input costs and selling price increases moderated but remained elevated, reinforcing concerns that inflation could persist above the Federal Reserve's target. The figures followed Friday's University of Michigan consumer sentiment report, which indicated that one-year inflation expectations declined to 3.7% from 4.7% in October , while longer-term expectations eased to 3.3% from 3.5%. The combination of slowing business activity and persistent price pressure continued to complicate the outlook for monetary policy.
Market positioning remains heavily tilted toward another Federal Reserve interest rate increase at the Dec. 8-9 meeting, with the latest published futures assessment indicating approximately a 95% probability of a 25-basis-point increase and a 5% probability of a larger 50-basis-point move. New York Fed President John Williams reinforced expectations for additional tightening Monday, emphasizing the persistence of elevated inflation despite some moderation in economic activity. The dollar remained near its strongest levels since April 2025, while the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield traded near the 4.9% area following last week's substantial decline. Investors now turn to Tuesday's September house price figures at 9 a.m. EST, followed by November consumer confidence and the Richmond Fed manufacturing survey at 10 a.m. EST. Wednesday's more consequential releases include October personal consumption expenditures inflation, durable goods orders and the second estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product at 8:30 a.m. EST, followed by the Fed's Beige Book at 2 p.m. EST. The PCE report could significantly influence December rate expectations, Treasury yields and the dollar. Stronger-than-expected inflation would reinforce the case for further tightening and pressure gold, while softer price readings could support a recovery in precious metals.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remains highly uncertain Tuesday as renewed attacks on commercial shipping and stalled diplomatic negotiations maintain significant risks to regional petroleum exports. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed Monday that three oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines in the strategic waterway, although the circumstances of the incidents have not been independently established. The United States is also investigating possible Iranian involvement in cyberattacks targeting energy tankers. Commercial shipping slowed sharply following last week's attacks on vessels operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, with vessel-tracking figures indicating only five commodity ships transited the strait Saturday and none were recorded Sunday, compared with 31 during the preceding weekend. Some vessels may have operated without active tracking signals, but the decline nevertheless highlighted continuing security concerns. Tehran has ruled out renewed negotiations with Washington until several conditions are met, including an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and relief from sanctions. For gold, the unresolved confrontation supports underlying defensive demand, although expectations for restrictive Federal Reserve policy and dollar strength continue to limit the metal's response to geopolitical risks.
Crude oil prices declined Tuesday as expectations for recovering global petroleum supply and a potential market surplus offset concerns about renewed attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures traded near $89.10 a barrel in early European dealings, down approximately 0.3%, while Nymex WTI crude was near $79.97, also down around 0.3%. Both benchmarks approached their lowest levels in approximately three months as increasing inventories and recovering production reinforced expectations that supply growth could outpace demand. Global observed petroleum inventories increased by approximately 52 million barrels during October, suggesting a growing surplus despite continued Middle Eastern shipping disruptions. The reopening of Libya's Sharara oil pipeline also contributed to improving supply expectations. Lower crude prices could help moderate energy-driven inflation, although underlying U.S. price pressures remain the more immediate concern for Federal Reserve policy.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 3.01% to close at 49,595.31, while the S&P 500 surged 4.73% to 7,237.17 and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.51% to 24,089.56. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also rebounded, gaining 2.69% to finish at 34,082.12, as resource and technology shares recovered from the previous week's losses. European equities recorded their strongest session in approximately six months Monday, led by semiconductor and technology companies, although gains faded in Tuesday morning trading. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was little changed near 637, while technology shares weakened as investors reassessed the sustainability of the rebound. Asian equities advanced sharply Tuesday, with Japan's Nikkei rising nearly 4% and South Korea's Kospi gaining more than 6%, while Taiwan's benchmark surged almost 9%. items.content:
Figure caption, A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
By Rachel Clun Business reporter ,Â  Reporting from New York
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.
His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.
Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.
Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday , with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.
Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.
Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.
While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.
A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.
On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.
Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.
Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".
"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.
"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.
"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.
"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.
"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."
Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."
She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

items.content:
Fed's John Williams indicates higher interest rates likely 'over time' to address inflation
New York Fed President John Williams said Monday that the central bank has "work to do" on inflation that should be tackled "over time."
The remarks are largely consistent with the patient approach the influential policymaker has advocated.
John Williams, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, speaks during an Economic Club of New York (ECNY) event in New York, US, on Thursday, Sept. 4, 2025.
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Monday that policymakers have more work to do to bring inflation under control, though he indicated that further action can unfold over time as the economy continues to grow.
In remarks consistent with previous statements , the influential central banker expressed confidence that inflation will get closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027 before hitting the goal the following year. He also said that while artificial intelligence is pressuring prices, there's "little evidence" it will be the source of more persistent inflation.
"But getting inflation back to 2% is 100% essential," he said in remarks at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York. "We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done."
The comments come at a delicate moment for monetary policy, as the economy continues to grow and inflation stays well above the Fed's goal.
Fed officials have differed over how quickly to raise rates, with some advocating more aggressive action while others, including Williams, have emphasized a measured approach.
Williams ascribed the current inflation pressures to the conflict in Iran, demand for goods associated with the AI build-out and tariffs, the effects of which he said "have largely abated" as a source of pressure. Nevertheless, he expressed confidence that inflation will subside substantially in 2027 even as economic growth remains robust and unemployment edges lower.
The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Dec. 8-9, with markets fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate increase from the current target range of 3.75%-4%. The remarks from Williams are expected to be the last major policy statement from any Fed official before the December decision.
"Monetary policy cannot move ships or reopen pipelines and refineries, but it can — and must — ensure that these shocks do not lead to broader or persistent inflationary dynamics or erode well-anchored inflation expectations," Williams said, according to his prepared remarks.
Williams did not explicitly address the December meeting expectations, instead pointing to the statement released after the prior FOMC meeting in late October that said the "accumulation of more information" will help decide the future policy path.
"The data that we have received since then show that the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high," he said.

items.title: One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests - CNN
items.summary: One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests  CNN
items.content:
A monument to the dead overlooks a massive burial site of Russian soldiers in the rural Volga region of Kostroma, Russia, on October 20, 2025.
Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly one death every four minutes, analysis based on leaked official data has revealed.
Russian opposition outlets Mediazona and Meduza reported on Monday that by the end of September, 490,000 Russian troops had been confirmed dead by Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat.
But accounting for time lags in reporting and including troops who have been reported as missing in action – and are most likely dead – Russian fatalities jump to more than 720,000 since the start of the war, according to the two outlets.
That is a staggering number that surpasses Russia’s death toll from the Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s and both Chechen wars in the 1990s and early 2000s – and which the Kremlin has long tried to keep secret.
Rescue workers and a search dog comb through the rubble of an apartment building in Dymer, Kyiv region, Ukraine, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, a day after a Russian drone strike hit the building. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)
The Ukraine-Russia war is seeping out across Europe and there are two reasons it will get worse
Rosstat stopped publishing demographic data in 2025 to disguise the rising death toll from the war. Mediazona and Meduza, as well as other outlets, obtained the official data after two pro-Ukrainian hacker groups, Cyber ​​Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, managed to breach Rosstat’s servers earlier this month.
CNN cannot independently verify the figures, but the leaked data on confirmed deaths alone corroborates earlier estimates by analysts and Western intelligence – which now appear to fall far short of the likely real death toll.
Mediazona and Meduza have long been keeping a tally of Russian losses, based mostly on inheritance documents, death notices and other publicly available documents.
Ukrainian servicemen fire a self-propelled howitzer towards Russian positions in eastern Ukraine on December 28, 2022.
But the leaked Rosstat data allowed the media outlets to go a step further, using the same methods and calculations normally employed by actuaries estimating risks and insurance premiums.
By analyzing discrepancies between reported death dates and death registration dates, and by comparing these to search notices published by relatives, the reporters were able to extrapolate the number of deaths that have occurred but have not yet been reported to be somewhere around 230,000.
Mediazona has kept a tally of troops identified as missing by their relatives from 2023. That database contains 160,000 individuals and almost all of them are likely dead. Mediazona said that based on its reporting, the rate of survival among those reported missing only around 10%.
The data shared by Silent Crow showed that the war was the fourth most common cause of death in Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion, after heart diseases; Covid; and stroke and other vascular conditions. It also confirms what has long been suspected – that the losses are not spread evenly across Russia, with poorer areas and ethnic minorities suffering significantly higher casualty rates.
In addition, an analysis by the NEST Centre, a think tank that also obtained the data, revealed the scale of Russia’s recruitment of foreign fighters. It identified 6,947 records of foreign nationals killed in Ukraine – the majority of them from the central Asian countries of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan.
Maria Pevchikh, the head of investigations at Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation, said the release of the data shows why Russian President Vladimir Putin is unlikely to seek compromise to end the war.
Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
“Putin has no way to ‘step back from public life’ or ‘focus on housing and utilities problems’ after killing 700,000 of his own citizens, and he never will. You don’t retire after something like that,” she said on X.
Meanwhile, Alexander Baunov, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, noted the war in Ukraine was Russia’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
“We talk a lot about the risk of nuclear escalation. But in terms of human losses, we may already be approaching the scale of a limited nuclear war,” he said.
Aby Shukiurov, a demographer and an associate fellow at the NEST Centre, said the Russian authorities “made concerted efforts to conceal the demographic reality of the war.”
Shukiurov pointed out that the high death toll has pushed down male life expectancy in Russia to 65.3 years in 2025. That is 3.1 years lower than in 2019 and almost at the level recorded in 2021, the worst year of the pandemic. Meanwhile, female life expectancy continued to rise during the war, reaching a record high of 79.3 years in 2025, he said.
Like Russia, Ukraine doesn’t release official casualty data, although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly acknowledged the scale of losses in combat. The most recent research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July that the country has endured between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities.
Baunov said that the combined death between Russia and Ukraine could exceed 1 million.
“One million dead is an important psychological threshold. But if almost nobody in Russia knows that this threshold may have been crossed, it is as if it hasn’t been crossed at all,” he said on X.
CNN’s Clare Sebastian and Nathan Hodge contributed reporting.

items.title: The ‘eighth front’: Why Israel’s influence war in the US is failing - Al Jazeera
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share The ‘eighth front’: Why Israel’s influence war in the US is failing on social media
US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at a joint news conference [File: Jim Watson/AFP]
Israeli efforts to maintain the public goodwill of its principal ally, the United States, appear to be continuing despite a series of setbacks.
According to filings with the US Department of Justice’s Foreign Agent Registration Act on October 28, US influencing company Starboard was contracted by Israeli firm LDRS Group LLC, which declares itself as acting on behalf of the State of Israel to conduct “strategic communications and public relations services in the United States to promote the interests of the State of Israel”.
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
list 2 of 4 Netanyahu is playing with the fire that killed Rabin
list 3 of 4 Could Iran reverse its stated policy of a civil-only nuclear programme?
list 4 of 4 Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
This builds on previous efforts to influence the US public. The Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft estimates that more than $1bn has been spent in direct funding for programmes to influence US public opinion in favour of Israel since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. That figure stands independent to the fundraising and political efforts of domestic organisations supporting Israel, such as the highly influential American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
US support for the multiple wars Israel has embarked on since the Hamas-led attack of 2023 has been close to unconditional. In addition to the annual grant, agreed under former President Barack Obama in 2016, the US has provided at least $25.5bn in appropriations and at least $21.7bn in military support, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project. Almost as critical has been the diplomatic support, which has seen the US use its veto t o block United Nations Security Council ceasefire resolutions as well as allowing Palestinian full UN membership.
However, evidence that US public support for Israel is collapsing is growing and has, for lawmakers in both countries, become unavoidable. Numerous polls point to growing hostility to Israel, especially among the young, stretching to include those on the right who hold Israel responsible for gulling President Donald Trump into an unwinnable war with Iran that is forcing their own cost of living, and gas prices, still higher.
A banner depicting US President Donald Trump (2-L), Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (2-R), US Vice President JD Vance (R) and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, on a street in Tehran, Iran, November 3, 2026 [Majid Asgaripour/WANA] President Donald Trump’s announcement that the US would end an Obama-era grant to Israel early, made on the day of the US midterms, was widely seen as an attempt to stave off the worst consequences of waning support for Israel across the political divide. But it did little to halt the rout that followed. The heavy spending by AIPAC and its affiliated organisations, estimated at $84m, in support of explicitly pro-Israel candidates, such as Senator Susan Collins of Maine, was largely considered a waste .
“The shift that has occurred in American public attitudes toward Israel is paradigmatic, generational, and lasting,” pollster Shibley Telhami, the director of the University of Maryland’s Critical Issues Poll, said.
“You cannot unsee what you saw in Gaza, over three years. Israeli public relations campaigns are thus swimming against the tide. When they are visibly connected to Israel, they are even toxic, achieving the opposite results, as we have seen in the midterm elections.”
The pro-Israel campaigns are seeing the biggest impact among Republicans, especially among the Evangelical right. “But even there, there is evidence younger people are less impacted by these active and expensive campaigns,” Telhami said.
Concerns that Israel may be losing the battle for American hearts and minds reach beyond the state’s traditional allies on the right. Speaking with US media in May, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attributed the loss of US public support to unspecified foreign states’ manipulation of social media, ignoring the genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 70,000 people, including about 20,000 children, in the past three years. He characterised this as an “eighth front” in Israel’s ongoing wars with regional powers.
Displaced Palestinian children participate in a ‘Will and Life’ race in Jabalia, northern Gaza Strip, on November 22, 2026 [AFP] In March, Israel quadrupled the budget for its public diplomacy or “hasbara”, to $730m, much of it earmarked for US social media and American eyeballs. In November, it appeared to go further, bringing more than 250 of what Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs determined to be the next generation of US officials, journalists, influencers and community leaders to tour sites associated with the October 7 attack and cement relations with leading Israeli officials.
“Quadrupling the hasbara spend just means they’re more stupid than I thought they were and I already thought they were pretty stupid,” former Israeli ambassador and consul general in New York Alon Pinkas said. “You change the conversation by changing the policy … So far, they haven’t let any foreign media into Gaza. Can you imagine what happens when they do? No amount of spending on their social media is going to mitigate what international journalists find there.”
Israel and its place in the Middle East had already been losing their relevance to the US before the war on Gaza, he said.
Washington had achieved energy security, the bogeyman of the USSR had been consigned to history, China had emerged as an area of critical interest, and both the public and politicians had grown weary of the kind of forever wars, he said, such as the current US-Israel war on Iran that shows no signs of ending.
“Add to that a resentful and angry president in the White House, and you have some idea of the job [potential incoming prime minister, [Gadi] Eisenkot or whoever, has ahead of them: One that no amount of Hasbara is really going to help.”
US President Donald Trump holds hands and speaks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, in Jerusalem on October 13, 2025 [AFP] Long-term damage?
How far Israeli efforts to entrench US support among future leaders, or to game the country’s social media platforms, might go in reversing negative perceptions of Israel among the American public remains unclear. The midterm elections saw several of the country’s most vocal critics of Israel elected to Congress.
The prospect of renewed war with Iran, initiated through a partnership of two deeply unpopular leaders in the US and Israel, is unlikely to win hearts and minds.
“There’s no doubt that the three pillars of US support for Israel – the public, congressional, and the executive – are at an all-time low, certainly the lowest in my experience,” former State Department Middle East negotiator Aaron David Miller, now a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment, said.
“It’s not just that we’ve seen the US engage in talks over Israel’s advice with Hamas, Yemen’s Houthi rebels and zeroing out aid [in] US weapons, but we’ve also seen a US president talk of his Israeli counterpart in extraordinary terms, and allowing highly critical phone calls of him discussing him to be leaked. However, this doesn’t mean we’re looking at a permanent rupture. A new Israeli government following different policies will take a good part of the tension out of public perceptions and Congressional angst.”

items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share Iran files lawsuits in US, EU courts: Will it get justice for ‘war crimes’? on social media
Women mourning in Minab following the school attack in February which Iran says was a war crime [File: Majid Saeedi/Getty Images]
Iran has filed lawsuits in the United States and European countries for alleged war crimes committed during the US-Israel war, including the missile attack on a school that killed at least 178 people, most of them schoolgirls.
Vice President for Legal Affairs Majid Ansari said on Sunday that Iran has begun legal proceedings in courts in the US and four European countries over “war crimes”, months after the deadly attack on a primary school in Minab in February on the first day of the ongoing war .
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 United Nations says US may have committed war crimes in Iran: What it means
list 2 of 4 Iran’s Pezeshkian slams ‘terrorist’ US but extols diplomacy in UN speech
list 3 of 4 Iran’s children return to school under the shadow of war
list 4 of 4 Iranians fear more civilian infrastructure could be targeted in new US war
The lawsuits will cover the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei , Iran’s official news agency IRNA reported. They will also address the deaths of scientists, military commanders and civilians, as well as attacks on civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, ambulances and emergency facilities.
Speaking at a ceremony honouring the families of children killed in US and Israeli attacks, Ansari said his office is working with the country’s justice and foreign ministries to pursue claims under international law.
The courts in the US and European countries have not been identified, but Ansari said proceedings had been initiated in courts that accepted jurisdiction over the cases. He gave no further specific details.
Experts say the cases in Europe may offer a more viable legal avenue, while proceedings in the US face significant jurisdictional hurdles. But whether Iran can turn these proceedings into meaningful accountability is questionable.
“Iran is pursuing the legal avenues available to it, seeking accountability and preserving evidence,” Saeed Bagheri, an assistant professor in international law at the University of Reading in the UK, told Al Jazeera.
“Compensation may be an objective, but it is far from assured.”
Iran is pursuing its cases in the US and Europe because it has limited access to international courts.
Ansari said Iran was considering filing a case with the International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries individuals charged with the most grave crimes. But Tehran – alongside the US and Israel – is not a signatory to the Rome Statute under which the court was formed in 2002. Iran would, therefore, need an independent basis for jurisdiction, such as a UN Security Council referral.
At the International Court of Justice (ICJ) – the world’s top court that handles legal disputes between states – jurisdiction depends on state consent under Article 36 of the ICJ, said Bagheri.
“Iran cannot simply demand a hearing in either court,” said the expert, who is also a fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law based in Germany.
Amid the legal hurdles, Iran has filed a number of cases in both domestic and international courts accusing the US and Israel of committing war crimes in the June 2025 war as well as the ongoing war. Iran says more than 3,500 people have been killed and 26,500 wounded in the war, along with widespread damage to civilian infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, bridges and energy facilities.
In March, Iran filed a complaint at the Iran-US Claims Tribunal in The Hague, accusing Washington of military aggression, illegal economic sanctions and threats of force. The Tribunal was formed following the 1981 Algiers Accords brokered by Algeria.
On Sunday, Ansari said preparations were under way for a second complaint to the Tribunal over the current war.
In September, Iran’s judiciary issued indictments against 159 senior US and Israeli political and military officials over the assassination of Khamenei and military commanders, judiciary spokesman Ali Kazemi said.
The Iranian judiciary has also said that about 400 cases have been filed with Iranian courts as part of domestic and international legal proceedings, including one involving 350,000 plaintiffs, Press TV reported.
A judiciary official on Monday said that local courts have demanded $290bn in damages from the United States.
A separate civil lawsuit was filed in the US in September by the National Iranian American Council Action (NIAC), a US civil society organisation, alongside several Iranian plaintiffs, including the father of a girl killed in the Minab school bombing. The case seeks a ruling that the US military campaign in Iran was unconstitutional. This case was not brought by the Iranian government.
The Minab school bombing is a large component of Iran’s pursuit of justice in the US and European courts.
In September, a report by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission found that the United States likely committed “war crimes” when it struck the school.
But Iran’s arsenal of evidence to prove that the Minab school bombing was a war crime would have to be wide in scope – civilian deaths do not, on their own, establish a war crime, said Bagheri in Reading.
Iran would need to establish who carried out the attack, what was targeted and what the relevant decision-makers knew at the time, he explained.
Calling a strike accidental also does not settle whether it was lawful or not, said Bagheri.
Investigators must assess whether the military followed the rules of distinction, proportionality and precautions to protect civilians, he added.
“For Minab, the crucial evidence would include targeting files, intelligence assessments, no-strike lists, collateral-damage estimates and records showing when the information was last verified,” Bagheri explained.
According to the UN Mission’s report, the civilian nature of the school was apparent and the US failed in its obligation “to do everything feasible” to verify that it was a military objective.
The report’s authors said that photographs and videos depicting the school before and after the attack showed “readily identifiable features” that it was associated with an educational facility for young children.
“According to public reporting, satellite imagery of the school before the strike also appears to show human figures, readily identifiable as children, gathered in its courtyard,” the report said.
Ultimately, the biggest challenge, said Bagheri, would be linking the evidence of what happened to the decisions, knowledge and intentions of specific military commanders or officials, rather than simply establishing that civilians were killed.
In June, US President Donald Trump said that “nobody” purposefully attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident, for which the Pentagon has not yet published any findings.
The Pentagon launched an internal investigation, but it has not yet publicly released its report.
Both the US and Israeli states, as well as individual officials and military commanders, could potentially be held responsible for the alleged violations, but under different legal frameworks.
State responsibility depends on whether an action can be attributed to a state and whether it breached international law, said Bagheri.
Individual criminal responsibility, meanwhile, can extend to those who carried out, ordered or assisted crimes, as well as commanders who failed to prevent or respond to crimes by forces under their effective control, the expert said.
Rank alone does not matter and investigators must establish what individuals knew, what authority they exercised and what they could have done, said Bagheri.
Still, immunity may also shield some officials from prosecution in foreign courts, particularly serving heads of state, government leaders and foreign ministers.
“Functional immunity for other officials accused of international crimes is more contested and depends on the forum,” said the expert from the University of Reading.
“But I would treat Khamenei’s killing separately. Article 110 of Iran’s Constitution gives the supreme leader command authority, but that title alone does not settle whether he was lawfully targetable.”
His actual military role and the circumstances of the attack matter, he added.
Iran may have a more viable path to pursuing its cases in Europe than in the US.
In some European countries, prosecutors can pursue serious international crimes under universal jurisdiction, regardless of the nationality of the accused or where the alleged offences happened.
But, Bagheri stressed, this route could lead to the prosecution of individuals – not a criminal trial of the US or Israeli governments.
The majority of European Union member states practice universal jurisdiction, according to the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation (Eurojust). The principle of universal jurisdiction allows the prosecution of individuals suspected of international crimes regardless of where they are committed.
In recent years, EU member states have been successful in bringing a number of perpetrators of international crimes to court on the basis of universal or extraterritorial jurisdiction, with convictions obtained in situations as diverse as Syria, Afghanistan, Rwanda and Liberia, including for crimes dating back 40 years, reports Eurojust.
Still, EU countries have varying requirements to proceed with a case, spanning their own presence, residence, nationality or territorial requirements, said Bagheri.
In his view, victims or civil parties are more likely to find success in producing investigations and preserving evidence than bringing senior US or Israeli officials to trial.
In the US, however, Iran faces “serious obstacles” in pursuing its cases, Bagheri said.
“That does not make them pointless, but getting a complaint before a court is a long way from securing a trial or compensation,” he said.
The first obstacle is sovereign immunity – the country’s Federal Tort Claims Act excludes claims arising in a foreign country and claims arising from combatant activities during wartime, said Bagheri.
Suing individual officials may not get around those protections either, he added.
The US War Crimes Act allows prosecution for certain offences, but neither Iran nor victims can initiate federal criminal cases themselves – that decision rests with US prosecutors, said Bagheri.
Experts point out that securing compensation could prove even more difficult than obtaining an investigation or court judgement.
State property may be immune from seizure, while a company’s links to a defendant do not automatically make its assets available to satisfy a judgement. US sanctions on Iran could further complicate payments, Bagheri said.
An arrest warrant, Bagheri said, does not guarantee that a suspect will be detained. Suspects generally must enter a country willing and legally able to act, he said, adding that an Interpol Red Notice is not an international arrest warrant and does not compel an arrest.
Despite these obstacles, Bagheri said Iran’s proceedings could still serve the purpose: preserving evidence and, where courts reach the merits, establishing legal responsibility.

items.title: China has changed tactics but is still thwarting India's rise, a U.S. panel says - CNBC
