items.content:
China has changed tactics but still thwarts India's rise: U.S. panel
The USCC panel report last week warned that China is "actively working" to suppress India's rise, applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure.
Tensions between India and China create opportunities for the U.S. to develop ties with India to counter Beijing's growing influence.
Experts agree that China is thwarting India’s growth but add that India is unlikely to align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
A conceptual image depicting the strained relationship between India and China, symbolized by their respective national flags painted on cracked and weathered surfaces, separated by a jagged, dividing line.
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

items.content:
Amazon has agreed to acquire AI startup Decart's key software and three cofounders, along with much of its top talent, the company announced.
Founded in 2023, the Israeli company is best known for its software that lets developers sync their AI models across different chips.
It marks the latest example of major tech companies acquiring pieces of buzzy AI startups.
Amazon logo on brick office building facade with windows, San Francisco, California, Aug. 29, 2025.
Smith Collection | Gado | Archive Photos | Getty Images
Amazon is scooping up much of the technology and talent behind artificial intelligence startup Decart, marking the latest reverse acquihire deal by a major tech company.
In a Monday blog post , Amazon said it agreed to purchase Decart's "proprietary technology" and hire the startup's three founders, as well as their AI researchers and engineers.
The Israeli startup, founded in 2023, is best known for its software that lets developers sync their AI models across different chips, allowing them to switch hardware quickly, known as the Decart Optimization Stack.
"Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip," Peter DeSantis, a senior vice president at Amazon who oversees foundation models, custom silicon and quantum computing development, said in a statement. "More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost."
DeSantis added, "From our earliest work with Decart, we knew they were the kind of technologically fearless team who would help us push it even further."
Nvidia skyrockets 30% on Huang’s return as CEO, recovering nearly all the losses since he disclosed affair
U.S. probes Megaspeed, Alice Huang as new figure emerges in Nvidia chip case
Anthropic's record IPO collides with tech's worst week on Wall Street since 2020
CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in $44 billion deal as AI supercharges cyberattacks
SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims
Amazon has moved deeper into building custom AI chips amid insatiable demand for the technology, and as companies seek alternatives to Nvidia , the dominant provider. Amazon has positioned its Trainium and Inferentia chips as lower-cost options for AI developers.
Last month, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said the company plans to make its Trainium chips externally available for the first time in "late in 2027."
Several outlets reported Amazon will pay $7.5 billion for Decart's assets, citing people familiar with the matter. Amazon declined to comment on the terms of the deal.
Anthropic had considered acquiring Decart and conducted due diligence, but ultimately walked away from a deal, Bloomberg reported.
Tech companies including Microsoft , Meta and Google have announced a series of deals with buzzy AI startups, which involve licensing their technology or nabbing their top talent and founders. The moves, often referred to as reverse acquihires , stop short of buying the companies outright. Amazon made two similar deals in 2024 when it brought on talent from Adept and Covariant .
The arrangements have attracted regulatory scrutiny in some cases. Amazon said Monday the Decart deal is subject to regulatory approval.

Oil touches three-month lows as rising supply offsets Hormuz threat
A view of the commercial ships and oil tankers waiting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the most important strategic waterways for global trade, seen from the Gulf of Oman on November 19, 2026.
Oil prices ⁠fell to three-month lows on Tuesday on signs of rising crude supply and a potential market surplus, though risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz ​persisted.
Brent crude futures were down 75 ​cents, or 0.8%, at $88.62 a ​barrel by 0915 GMT, after hitting its lowest since August 27. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were 64 cents, or 0.8%, lower at $79.53 a barrel, after falling to the weakest since August 10.
"Oil prices are facing modest downward pressure from two sides: markets ⁠are ‌pricing out some near-term geopolitical risk in the Middle East, while releases ⁠from strategic reserves are keeping supply relatively comfortable despite lower regional exports and stronger Chinese demand," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
"Brent has largely lost any upward impetus in recent days as supply conditions remain benign despite the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and the market weighs the possibility of ‌a future supply glut against persistent Middle East tensions and shipping disruptions."
However, Suvro Sarkar, head of energy research at DBS Bank, said prices risk going higher again depending on talks between the US and Iran and ​as both parties could test the other's resolve in blockading the strait.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said three "violating" oil tankers had caught fire after hitting naval mines in the strait on Monday, Iran's Press TV reported.
The United States is also investigating whether Iran was involved in cyberattacks on as many as 50 energy tankers, the Wall Street ⁠Journal reported, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter.
Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has reopened after an "unlawful group" closed a valve on ‌the pipeline, and oil has begun to flow into storage tanks at the Akakus ‌facility in Zawiya, the chairperson of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Monday.
China and India are on track for record Russian oil imports this year, plugging a supply gap shortage caused by the Iran war, according to tanker data and industry sources.
Temporary US waivers on Russian ⁠oil sanctions, aimed at keeping markets supplied amid the Middle East crisis, widened the pool of vessels and ⁠suppliers available to India and China, allowing them to increase purchases.
While better supply is weighing on prices, ⁠analysts said the market remained fragile.
"Oil prices, time spreads, refining margins and investor positioning increasingly suggest the market expects conditions to normalise," Daniel Hynes, senior commodity strategist at ANZ, said in a client note. "Yet ​logistics remain constrained and inventory buffers are thin."
Deutsche Bank said ‌that global observed liquids' inventory rose in October, implying an oversupply of 1.7 million barrels each day. Evidence is accumulating that the global market is rebalancing and turning into surplus, although setbacks could delay progress, the bank said in a research report.
US crude oil and product inventories likely rose last week, a preliminary Reuters poll showed.
Elsewhere, Iraq's prime minister has ordered the federal oil ministry to manage oilfields in ​areas under Kurdish security control, the state news agency ‌said on Tuesday, potentially deepening tensions between Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region.

items.summary: Jensen Huang Just Killed Hopes For a Fed Rate Pause. Will Kevin Warsh Crush the Stock Market Recovery on Dec. 9?  <font color="#6f6f6f"
items.content:
The probability that the Fed would hold rates steady at its Dec. 9 meeting went to zero after Jensen Huang was reinstated.
Concerns about rising bond yields at CoreWeave helped spark the AI sell-off.
Fed rate hikes are a risk that AI investors shouldn't ignore.
Investors cheered as Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia ( NVDA +31.48% ) , reinstated as CEO of the company he led for 33 years.
The Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.5%, and the S&P 500 gained 4.9% on Monday, as it seemed like the fears that crushed the stock market last week had suddenly vanished.
However, the return of Huang and the subsequent stock market surge bring other risks. With the stock market in free fall last week, investors were starting to hedge their bets that the Fed would raise rates at its next meeting on Dec. 9. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, bets that the Fed would hold interest rates steady grew last week as the market crashed, reaching an 11.4% chance of no change at the next meeting.
On Monday, after Huang's return, that probability fell to zero, and investors now see a 4.9% chance that the Fed hikes rates by 50 basis points. Some Fed Governors, like Christopher Waller, have argued for a 50-basis-point hike at the next meeting.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.
The Fed has a dual mandate to maximize employment and keep prices stable, as reflected in its 2% inflation target.
In other words, the Fed isn't supposed to directly consider the stock market, but the stock market impacts both employment and inflation. It represents trillions of dollars of wealth, and when the stock market falls sharply, like it did last week, investors are less likely to spend money, and falling stock prices could put pressure on businesses as well, leading to layoffs.
The Fed monitors asset prices, including stock prices, but Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has made it clear that taming inflation is his top priority, as inflation has been above the Fed's target for five years.
Rate hikes tend to cool off the stock market as higher interest rates raise borrowing costs for businesses and also entice investors to rotate from stocks into bonds.
With expectations for a December rate hike now built in, the impact of a 25-basis-point hike should be mostly priced in to the market, though the probability of a rate hike could change after the October PCE report comes out on Wednesday.
Fed rate hikes, which are expected to continue into next year, are likely to exacerbate one of the biggest issues in the AI sector .
Concerns about rising yields on CoreWeave's bonds sparked the start of the sell-off in AI stocks last October, and that pressure remains. In fact, one of the issues surrounding Huang's departure was that he was behind many of the financial backstop arrangements that Nvidia had made with companies like CoreWeave . Those promises are propping up a significant portion of the AI sector, as Nvidia holds stakes in several AI stocks and start-ups and has complex financing arrangements with companies that buy its chips.

We don't know what the stock market will do in the two weeks between now and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Dec. 9, and if stocks continue to rally, the Fed will have more leeway to raise rates.
However, last week's plunge shows how jittery investors are and how fragile the AI boom has become, as prior to Huang's resignation, investors were already bailing on AI stocks, first over solvency concerns at CoreWeave and other neoclouds and then over the backlash against data centers in the midterm election.
Those issues haven't changed because Huang is back at Nvidia, though investors may be willing to put them aside for now.
If selling pressure returns to the AI sector, any rate hikes from the Fed will only add fuel to the fire, regardless of expectations or the impact on inflation.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures are sliding on Tuesday morning, November 24, 2026, as Wall Street cools off from Monday’s blistering tech rally and shifts its focus back to Federal Reserve rate-hike risks, fresh Iran sanctions, and crucial inflation data due before the Thanksgiving holiday.
Early premarket trading shows losses concentrated heavily in technology and artificial intelligence shares , while the blue-chip Dow is experiencing a more modest pullback ahead of the 9:30 a.m. ET opening bell.
As of roughly 7:04 to 7:33 a.m. ET, all three major U.S. equity index futures were trading in the red:
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures (YM=F): Down 0.5% to 0.57% (shedding roughly 281 points to trade near 49,396).
S&P 500 futures (ES=F): Down roughly 0.85% to 1% (falling more than 61 points).
Nasdaq-100 futures (NQ=F): Leading the decline, down 1.64% to 2% (dropping roughly 440 points).
Standout premarket movers: Nvidia (NVDA) dropped roughly 4.9% to 5.2%, dragging down chipmakers Micron, AMD, and Marvell (down 3.9% to 6.4%) and AI cloud names CoreWeave (-5.8%) and Nebius (-6.1%). Anthropic (ANT) fell around 4.4% to 5%, briefly slipping below its $83 IPO price on track for a third straight daily decline. Meanwhile, Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) tumbled roughly 11% to 12% after Q4 results, while retail bright spots Best Buy (BBY) (+5% to 6.7%) and Dollar Tree (DLTR) (+8.6%) jumped on strong outlooks.
Profit-taking cools Monday’s historic Nvidia-fueled rally
Tuesday’s dip is largely a breather after one of Wall Street’s most explosive sessions in years. On Monday, November 23, the Dow surged 3.01%, the S&P 500 jumped 4.73%, and the Nasdaq Composite soared 6.51% —marking the biggest single-day gains for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq since April 2025.
That rally was triggered by Nvidia’s stunning decision to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO , which sent Nvidia shares skyrocketing 31.5% —its best day in 23 years—and restored nearly $1 trillion in market value. Still, a nalysts say Huang’s return does not erase deeper investor jitters over debt-funded AI data center spending , regulatory scrutiny, or Huang’s upcoming congressional testimony on December 3.
FILE PHOTO: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, attends the US-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington, DC, US, November 19, 2025. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein//File Photo
"Nvidia’s stock price decline on Tuesday is to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. "The return of Huang does not mean that the challenges facing AI are over."
Fed rate-hike fears and fresh Iran sanctions weigh on sentiment
Beyond tech profit-taking, macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds are pressuring futures. Traders are now pricing in a 95% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Federal Reserve’s December 8–9 meeting—along with a 5% chance of a jumbo 50-basis-point increase, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. New York Fed President John Williams reinforced those concerns Monday, stating that persistently high inflation points toward tighter monetary policy.
The rapid whipsaw in AI stocks is also testing Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, with Evercore ISI’s Krishna Guha warning that talk of faster tightening adds stress while Warsh’s silence leaves markets guessing on his stance. The rate-sensitive 2-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.67%.
Geopolitical tensions added another layer of caution after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new U.S. sanctions targeting Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel, alongside reports of tanker incidents east of the Strait of Hormuz. Even so, energy and metals traded lower early Tuesday, with Brent crude dipping to $88.75 a barrel (near a three-month low), gold easing to $3,619.70 an ounce, and copper giving back 3%.
Is a market crash coming? Putting Tuesday’s drop in perspective
While steep red numbers in premarket trading can look alarming, strategists emphasize that Tuesday’s pullback is not a market crash—and gives back only a fraction of Monday’s massive gains. Even a 1.5% to 2% dip in Nasdaq futures barely dents the index’s 6.5% surge from the prior session.
Overseas markets also reflected lingering momentum from Monday’s U.S. rebound: Taiwanese shares rallied 9% (with TSMC and Foxconn nearing their 10% daily limits), South Korea’s Kospi jumped roughly 6.3% to 7%, and Japan’s Nikkei climbed nearly 4%, while Europe’s STOXX 600 slipped just 0.1%. Because premarket futures trade on thinner volume overnight, early losses can still narrow—or reverse—once regular U.S. trading begins at 9:30 a.m. ET.
What investors are watching next this Thanksgiving week
Trading volume is expected to thin out as the holiday approaches, with several key catalysts still on deck:
Tuesday’s data and earnings: Investors are tracking the Conference Board’s November Consumer Confidence reading (92.1 expected), ADP weekly employment figures, and the FHFA house price index, alongside earnings from Dell Technologies, HP, Dick’s Sporting Goods, Workday, and Autodesk.
Wednesday, November 25: Release of the PCE inflation report—the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge and the final major data point before December’s rate decision.
Thursday, November 26: U.S. stock markets (NYSE and Nasdaq) are closed for Thanksgiving.
Friday, November 27: Markets reopen for a shortened Black Friday session, closing early at 1:00 p.m. ET.

items.summary: The UK is joined by several other nations in recognising an ICJ ruling that Myanmar carried out genocide.
items.content:
Image caption, More than a million people were forced to flee the violence across the border to Bangladesh in 2017
The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that the country had carried out genocide against the Rohingya minority â marking the first time a state has been found guilty of the crime .
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.
The UK is joined by several other countries , external in acknowledging the ICJ ruling, including Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Canada.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action."
Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.
Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing , who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.
He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."
Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".
The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attachÃ© after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.
He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention , external .
In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.
Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi , was deposed by the military in 2021.

Refined fuels, which rallied even harder than crude and fanned global inflationary fears, have lost ground too. A barometer that approximates the cost of turning crude into gasoline and diesel — the so-called 3-2-1 crack — was the weakest since March as prices broadly retreated.

items.content:
Wall Street Futures Stabilise Following Nvidia Rebound as Fed Policy and Technology Earnings Remain in Focus: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq
Nasdaq sign on building ©Adobe Stock Images US equity futures fluctuated around unchanged levels on Tuesday after a substantial recovery in global stock markets following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).
Investors were also assessing the outlook for US monetary policy, quarterly results from Hewlett Packard Enterprise and expectations of a global oil supply surplus.
Nvidia Leadership Announcement Drives Global Equity Recovery
Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in Tuesday's premarket session after advancing more than 30% on Monday, an increase that added over US$1 trillion to the semiconductor manufacturer's market value.
The recovery followed the announcement that Huang would return as chief executive, having resigned approximately two weeks earlier.
The development supported widespread gains across Wall Street, particularly among technology companies exposed to artificial intelligence investment.
The Nasdaq Composite finished Monday's session 6.51% higher, while the S&P 500 gained 4.73% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 3.01%.
The session represented the strongest performance for US equity markets since April 2025.
"Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO lifted stocks on Monday and cleared the negative sentiment, opening room for a near-term rebound," analysts at BCA Research said in a research note.
Asian semiconductor-related markets recorded substantial increases following Monday's recovery in US technology stocks.
Taiwanese equities advanced 8.99%, while South Korea's KOSPI index gained 6.32%, reflecting renewed investor interest in companies supplying components for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Nvidia's expansion under Huang has positioned the company as a major supplier of advanced processors for AI datacentres, alongside its established gaming semiconductor operations.
The company has also supported investment across the AI industry through commercial and financing arrangements, some involving its own customers.
Despite the recovery in technology shares, uncertainty remains regarding the returns on AI infrastructure expenditure, the industry's reliance on debt financing and the future pace of US datacentre development.
Huang is expected to appear before US congressional committees, where Nvidia's business relationships with China and adherence to export restrictions could be examined.
Federal Reserve Rate Expectations Remain Elevated Ahead of December Meeting
Financial markets continue to anticipate a further increase in US interest rates at the Federal Reserve's December policy meeting.
The central bank raised rates by 25 basis points in October, marking its first increase in borrowing costs since 2023.
Minutes from that meeting indicated that most policymakers considered additional monetary tightening necessary to address inflationary pressures, driven in large part by higher energy costs associated with the conflict involving Iran.
A Federal Reserve governor has also indicated that a 50-basis-point increase could be warranted.
However, comments from New York Federal Reserve President John Williams on Monday suggested a more moderate assessment of the inflation outlook.
Williams noted that inflationary pressures associated with tariffs had eased, while housing services price growth had slowed.
"Inflation expectations remain well anchored," Williams argued, adding that he expects price growth to slow to just above the Fed's 2% target level in 2027.
The prospect of higher interest rates remains relevant to technology sector valuations, particularly for businesses relying on debt to finance infrastructure investment.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise Announces US$5 Billion Additional Share Buyback
Hewlett Packard Enterprise (NYSE:HPE) reported fiscal fourth-quarter financial results that exceeded market expectations, although its shares declined more than 9% in Tuesday's premarket trading.
The decline followed a gain of more than 17% during Monday's session.
Fourth-quarter revenue reached US$14.55 billion, while free cash flow totalled US$1.92 billion. Both figures exceeded consensus estimates cited by CNBC.
Analysts at Vital Knowledge attributed the performance to HPE's cloud and artificial intelligence operations, where sales increased by approximately 69% and orders more than doubled.
For the current quarter, HPE forecasts revenue of between US$14 billion and US$14.6 billion, alongside adjusted earnings per share of between US$1.30 and US$1.40.
The company's fiscal 2027 revenue and earnings projections also exceeded analyst expectations.
In addition, HPE announced a further US$5 billion share repurchase programme.
Analysts at Vital Knowledge nevertheless pointed to uncertainty surrounding longer-term capital expenditure across the AI industry, including whether investment spending could stabilise in 2028 as additional manufacturing capacity becomes operational.
Oil Prices Extend Declines as Global Supply Forecasts Increase
Crude oil prices remained under pressure on Tuesday as forecasts of excess supply continued to influence market sentiment despite ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
Brent crude traded at approximately US$88 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude futures stood at around US$79 per barrel.
The International Energy Agency recently projected that global oil supply would exceed demand by two million barrels per day during the final quarter of 2026, supported by recovering exports from the Gulf region.
Regional oil producers have been developing alternative export routes to mitigate supply disruptions, while US military forces have provided security for some vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
Goldman Sachs has forecast that continued improvements in regional export capacity could contribute to a substantial oil supply surplus during 2027.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte is seeking to reassure the alliance's eastern European members after three Russian cruise missiles landed in Poland on Friday.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST: Russian incursions into NATO territory are increasing. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte is seeking to reassure the alliance's Eastern European members after three Russian cruise missiles landed in Poland on Friday. While no one was hurt, Rutte was in Germany today, where he addressed growing concerns. And for more, we are joined now by Esme Nicholson in Berlin. Hey, Esme. ESME NICHOLSON, BYLINE: Hey, Scott. DETROW: The cruise missiles hit Poland during one of Russia's biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion. Ukraine then hit back over the weekend. So first, bring us up to speed on that. NICHOLSON: Well, as you say, the risks of the war in Ukraine spilling over were loud and clear over the weekend. It started on Friday morning with what Polish authorities have now identified as three Russian cruise missiles striking a rural part of southeastern Poland, about 30 miles from the Ukrainian border. Now, as you say, there were no casualties, but the incursions happened while European forces were staging a military exercise in the region. And Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk calls the incident an "intentional provocation" - that's a quote. Then on Saturday, a sanctioned Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea was hit by what is suspected to have been a Ukrainian maritime drone. And on Sunday, Ukraine took credit for sinking a Russian warship docked in the Libyan port of Benghazi, thousands of miles from the front line. Libyan authorities have condemned the attack in their port, reflecting broader concerns that the conflict could spread far beyond Europe. DETROW: Right. And that is a broad battlefield that you're talking about right there. NATO's chief was in Berlin today. Does he view this as the beginning of an escalation beyond Ukraine's borders? NICHOLSON: Well, Rutte was rather cautious in his assessment of the weekend. He was in Berlin for an annual meeting, talking to parliamentarians from NATO countries. And while he acknowledged the danger of cruise missile incursions, he was eager that Polish authorities finish their investigations to establish whether they were intentional or not. Speaking to journalists, he said the alliance has, quote, "many response options" (ph) but that he can't always be open about them. But he also appealed for public support for Ukraine. (SOUNDBITE OF PRESS CONFERENCE) MARK RUTTE: As societies, we have to be resilient and, most importantly, keep that support for Ukraine going. So for every incident in Europe, more support for Ukraine, not less support for Ukraine. NICHOLSON: And Zelenskyy, who dialed into the meeting in Berlin today, urged for fresh negotiations with Russia, this time involving the Europeans. DETROW: Let's talk more about the Europeans. What do you think the odds are that they'll end up playing a role in bringing about the end of this war? NICHOLSON: Well, since last week's coalition of the willing meeting here in Berlin, it's looking a little more likely. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and European leaders warned the U.S. and Russia against going over their heads. And today, Merz stressed that Europe is ready to sit at the table, something U.S. special envoy for peace missions Jared Kushner supports. But Merz also made it clear that no NATO member, quote, "has any interest in an escalation in the Baltic Sea region," which some see as an appeal to Ukraine to do its part to prevent the conflict from spreading. He vowed that European leaders would discuss boosting defense on NATO's eastern flank at an EU summit later this week. And he was also quite candid in stating that NATO made a mistake back in 2008 when it decided not to make Ukraine a member, saying that if Ukraine had been a NATO member, this war would probably have been preventable. DETROW: That is Esme Nicholson in Berlin. Thank you so much. NICHOLSON: Thank you, Scott.

items.title: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
items.summary: Days after resigning while mired in scandal of extra-marital affairs, Nvidia's Jensen Huang is making a remarkable return.
items.content:
By Michael Race ,Â  Peter Hoskins Â  and Â  Lucy Hooker ,Â  Business reporters
For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.
Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.
So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.
But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.
His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.
Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.
The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation
Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive?
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.
So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".
But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".
First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.
Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.
But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by an announcement that Huang was stepping down.
He'd barely been gone, however, before a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign was launched, reportedly by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.
The man himself said he would be "honoured" to return, should the board ask him.
Although initially showing no interest in reinstating him, the board has now done just that, saying his return was "in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

European Gas Prices Climb as Cold Snap Threatens Depleted Reserves
European benchmark natural gas prices rose on Tuesday for the fourth consecutive trading session as a cold snap this week is set to accelerate withdrawals from storage, where levels were at multi-year lows at the start of the heating season.
The front-month price at the Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) , the benchmark for Europe's gas trading, topped $98.77 (90.50 euros) per megawatt-hour (MWh) in the early morning in Amsterdam trade, rising by about 1% and extending the sharp gains from Monday.
Europe's natural gas prices soared by more than 8% at opening in Amsterdam on Monday, as weather model forecasts show colder weather coming to the continent, which is struggling with record-low inventories for this time of year.
The largest gas-consuming economies in northwest Europe, the UK, Germany, and France, will see freezing temperatures this week. This is set to raise gas demand for heating and electricity generation. Central and eastern Europe are also seeing an unusually bitter cold snap, which is expected to persist through the first week of December.
As a result of the early winter-like temperatures in most of Europe, gas inventories are expected to draw at a rapid pace over the next week or two, leaving lower volumes in storage for what are typically the coldest winter months.
The EU's gas storage sites were only 68.9% full as of November 23, compared to a five-year average of 89% and about 82% at this time last year, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe.
Before the heating season began, the most Europe managed was to have gas storage sites only about 76% full.
Net withdrawals from gas storage started in the middle of October and accelerated toward early November, before easing in the past two weeks, GIE data showed . However, the pace of withdrawals accelerated again this weekend and are set to continue at high rates at least until the end of the month.

Under the deal with VNG, announced on Tuesday, Equinor will supply up to 15.3 TWh, or around 1.4 billion cubic meters (bcm), of natural gas per year to VNG, starting on January 1, 2027.
Deliveries will continue until the end of 2044, and gas will be delivered at Trading Hub Europe, the German gas market area. Pricing will reflect market terms, while other commercial details are confidential between the parties, Equinor said.
The 18-year agreement with VNG is the longest gas sales agreement for Equinor since the Troll agreements were signed in 1986.
Germany is Equinor's largest market for natural gas and has been an anchor market for Norwegian gas since exports started in 1977.
With this agreement, VNG is strengthening its gas portfolio over the long term and contributing to secure and diversified gas supplies in Germany, the German firm said .
"Norwegian pipeline gas remains of great importance for a reliable supply of energy to Germany and Europe," said Ulf Heitmüller, CEO of VNG AG.
Earlier this year, Equinor also signed a 15-year natural gas sales agreement with Germany's Uniper, locking in more than 30 terawatt-hours of annual gas supplies to Europe's largest economy through 2041.
Norway tries to maintain a high level of oil and gas production and exports for at least another decade, to boost the economy and deliver oil and gas to Europe.
Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine cut off most Russian gas to Europe, Norway has become the single biggest supplier of gas to the EU and continues to be the largest supplier to the UK.
Equinor plans to drill 20 to 30 exploration wells every year as it aims to sustain current production levels at least through 2035, the company said in January when it was awarded 35 new production licenses on the Norwegian continental shelf in Norway's tender for mature exploration areas.

Gold coins and bars ©soofiatailor Gold prices declined on Tuesday as investors took profits following the previous session's recovery, while expectations of further Federal Reserve monetary tightening continued to weigh on bullion ahead of key US inflation data.
At 04:32 GMT, spot gold fell 0.3% to US$3,625.88 per ounce, while US gold futures declined 0.7% to US$3,624.90.
Other precious metals also weakened. Spot silver fell 1.3% to US$42.5855 per ounce, while platinum declined 1.8% to US$1,304.92.
Spot palladium dropped 0.9% to US$889.97, while palladium futures fell 1% to US$884.75. The US dollar index edged 0.04% lower to 104.30.
Gold had earlier advanced as much as 1% towards US$3,670 per ounce, following a 2.7% increase during Monday's session.
The recovery partially reversed last week's decline of nearly 9%, which pushed bullion to its lowest level in more than a year. Gold had also fallen below US$4,000 per ounce approximately two weeks earlier.
Improved investor sentiment followed Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, less than two weeks after his departure.

Financial markets continue to anticipate another interest rate increase at the Federal Reserve's December policy meeting.
Higher interest rates generally reduce the relative attractiveness of gold, which does not generate interest income.
Investors are also awaiting upcoming US inflation figures for further indications of the central bank's monetary policy direction.

The increase in gold purchases has also helped contain China's trade surplus with major trading partners, including the European Union.

"The fall in energy prices also spurred hope that inflation would be tamed in coming months, and thus ease pressure the Fed to hike rates," they said.

ANZ added that holdings in gold-backed exchange-traded funds had remained robust.

Nasdaq, Dow, S&P 500 Futures Gain As Jensen Huang’s Return To Nvidia Sparks $3T Market Rally: SOXS, IBRX, HPE, TSM In Focus
NVDA stock jumped 31.48% at close following the announcement, while other chipmakers also posted gains.
U.S. President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Nvidia has made "the correct and proper decision" to return Huang to the position of CEO.
However, some market participants flagged that this was a temporary boost and concerns still remained.
U.S. stock futures headed higher late Monday as the AI trade rebounded after Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) just two weeks after he was ousted amid reports of extramarital affairs.
As of 8:42 p.m. EST, Dow futures climbed 0.36%, while the S&P 500 futures gained 0.39% and Nasdaq-100 futures increased 0.49%.

On Monday, the three U.S. benchmark indexes closed significantly higher on the optimism. The Nasdaq Composite led the climb, adding nearly 1,500 points to close 6.51% higher. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed 3.01% up, and the S&P 500 gained 4.73%.
The reversal in markets followed a sharp selloff in markets last week as the AI trade faltered on rising concerns of its sustainability.
U.S. President Donald Trump congratulated Nvidia for its "absolutely GREAT decision" in a post on Truth Social.
Optimism on Wall Street soared after Nvidia announced that Huang would return as President, CEO, and board member of the company.
"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board, said in a statement.
"We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA's Chief Financial Officer."
NVDA stock jumped 31.48% at close following the announcement. Other AI stocks, including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Micron Technology Inc. (MU), and Intel Corp. (INTC) also saw a sharp increase in prices, riding on Nvidia's optimism.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) soared more than 13% on Monday, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) gained 15%. U.S. stocks added over $3 trillion in market capitalization.
Meanwhile, Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Nvidia has made "the correct and proper decision" to return Huang to the position of CEO.
"The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct," he said, adding that Nvidia should continue its thorough internal investigation of its compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations.
However, some market participants flagged that this was a temporary boost and concerns still remained.
Robin Brooks, Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution, said in a post on X, "There's a short-term sugar rush from Huang's return to Nvidia, but markets are sending 2 ominous signals: (i) USD is rising further away from rate differentials, so FX stress is mounting; (ii) oil is tumbling, so the Fed is getting more and more wrong…"
Brent crude futures were trading at $89.09 a barrel, down 0.31% at the time of writing, while WTI crude futures traded 0.17% lower at $80.03 per barrel.
The Kobeissi Letter noted in a post that while Huang's return is a huge win for the U.S. and the broader AI Revolution, Nvidia shares are still down 12% since the volatility started. It noted that the stock is also trading 33% below its record high.
The market commentator said that the broader AI trade is still experiencing growing pains as it undergoes a healthy technical correction but it continues to believe "that what has materialized over the last few weeks is a mere correction, not the beginning of a prolonged bear market."
"The AI Revolution is in full-swing, earnings growth is running at 32%+ year-over-year, and valuations have compressed significantly from their recent highs. Tune out the noise and this market becomes incredibly profitable."
Markets will also be watching closely for cues on the Federal Reserve's policy rate decision due in December.
According to data from the CME FedWatch tool, markets put the probability of a 25-basis-point hike in the December policy meeting at 95.1%, while odds of a 50 bps hike are at 4.9%.
On Monday, Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams highlighted inflation concerns and said that the central bank still has "work to do" to bring it under control.
In a speech at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York, Williams said that "We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis."
He also told reporters following the event that he "would not exclude moving at consecutive meetings at all if that was what was needed," as he continued to watch for signs of a stronger economy and strength on the supply side, as well as increases in gasoline prices that could add to inflation pressures.
On the economic front, on Wednesday, personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, will be released, providing further clues about the central bank's policy trajectory.
Meanwhile, the precious metals trade turned green on Monday following the widespread optimism on Wall Street.
Spot gold was up more than 1% to trade at $3,675.01 an ounce at the time of writing. Meanwhile, spot silver was up 1.55% to trade at $43.73 an ounce.
Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bear 3X ETF (SOXS): The inverse leveraged exchange-traded fund, which delivers approximately three times the opposite of the daily return of the NYSE Semiconductor Index, was down nearly 41% at close and continued to decline overnight amid the revival in the AI trade.
ImmunityBio (IBRX): The clinical-stage immunotherapy company was on the retail radar after it amended its revenue agreement to add a $65 million option and equities repayment feature before Dec. 31, 2027.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. (HPE): The company's shares slipped more than 6% in the overnight session after it reported fiscal fourth-quarter results . While revenue and profit surpassed Wall Street expectations, its Q1 FY27 outlook fell short of the high end of Wall Street's expectations.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM): The Asian chipmaker's shares jumped higher at close and continued to trade in green in the overnight session amid the jump in chip stocks and the AI sector after Huang's return to Nvidia.
Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was up 0.24% in the overnight session at the time of writing, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) gained 0.15% and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) edged 0.20% higher.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was trading at 4.932%, while the 30-year yield was at 5.299%.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was down 0.11% amid 'bullish' sentiment.
Asian markets opened higher on Tuesday. South Korea's KOSPI, China's SSE Composite index, Japan's Nikkei 225 and Australian stocks all traded in the green at the open.

Russia has accused Estonia of bringing the two countries to the brink of “open war.”
The Russian foreign ministry on Monday lodged a formal protest with the Estonian charge d’affaires in Moscow over Estonia’s decision to close its road border crossings with Russia. The ministry said the border closure was among several other “hostile” and “Russophobic” moves taken against Russia in recent years, adding that Russia reserves the right to respond with measures to protect its national interests.
“The Estonian diplomat was once again told that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of triggering ​open war with Russia,” the ministry said in a statement laying out the accusations.
“Tallinn apparently isn’t seriously considering the consequences of such a move,” the ministry warned.
Tensions between the Eastern European neighbors have sharply escalated since Estonia announced on Friday plans to close all road crossings with Russia for at least six months from December 1. Estonia’s decision came after it accused Russian intelligence of a foiled arson plot at an Estonian drone factory, which Moscow denied.
Estonian Charge d'Affaires Marek Uhtegi leaves the Russian Foreign Ministry headquarters in Moscow after being summoned over Estonia's closure of its shared border with Russia on Nov. 23, 2026. Kirill Zykov—Sputnik/AP
Estonia’s foreign minister Margus ​Tsahkna dismissed Russia’s claims and said Moscow is responsible for “the real security threats” in Europe.
“Russia is flooding ⁠the airwaves with baseless accusations against Estonia to distract from its own actions undermining European security,” Tsahkna posted on X on Monday.
As a member of both the NATO alliance and the European Union, Estonia would be entitled to assistance from members of both blocs if Russia launched an attack on Estonian territory. Asked about Russia’s accusations on Monday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said NATO was monitoring the security situation in Estonia and that the alliance had options to respond if needed.
Here’s what to know about the recent hostilities between Russia and Estonia.
Russia’s foreign ministry said Estonia’s decision to close their road border is the latest of “numerous hostile actions” taken against Russia.
It accused the Estonian government of “tacitly” allowing Ukraine to use its airspace to attack Russia.
Russia has previously accused Estonia and other NATO Baltic states of letting Ukrainian drones use their airspace. Since Russia invaded the country in February 2022, Ukrainian drones have entered NATO airspace on multiple occasions, although NATO countries have denied permitting drones to use their airspace. The Ukrainian government said the incursions were a result of diversions caused by Russian electronic warfare.
Estonia rejected the allegation in a statement on Monday.
“While we generally do not comment on or engage with Russian propaganda narratives, in this case we can reiterate that Estonia has never allowed, and will never allow, its territory to be used for military operations by another country,” Estonia’s foreign ministry told Reuters .
The Russian foreign ministry also accused Estonia of attempting to obstruct the movement of Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea, including trying to “inspect, seize, and detain them with the aim of imposing a naval blockade” on Russia.
Estonia’s navy boarded and detained a Russia-bound tanker in April 2025, saying it lacked a valid flag, and attempted to stop another Russia-bound tanker the following month. There is no official blockade, and a senior Estonian commander told Reuters in April that the navy would refrain from detaining Russia’s shadow fleet vessels because of the risk of a military confrontation.
Russia’s foreign ministry pointed to Estonia’s Oct. 8 ban on the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain through its territory as another example of a “hostile” action against Russia. The E.U. tariffs grain imports from Russia and Belarus, citing Russia’s seizure of Ukrainian grain, although it allows shipments to transit the E.U. Estonia’s foreign ministry said Russia was looking for alternatives to Black Sea export routes and that Estonia would preventively keep its ports from serving as an outlet for Russian grain and potential revenue to fund the war.
Russia’s foreign ministry also alleged that the Estonian government imposed oppressive measures on Russian-speaking residents in Estonia. Among the alleged actions are a ban on the Russian language “at all levels,” criminal prosecutions and deportations of Russia sympathizers, and the threat of dissolving a Russian orthodox church in Estonia.
Estonia did not respond to those allegations in its statement. There is no official ban on the Russian language in Estonia. The government mandates Estonian in official settings and is phasing out Russian as a main teaching language in some kindergartens and schools as part of a transition to Estonian-language instruction . Russian is the mother tongue of around 27% of Estonia’s population , according to government data.
The Estonian Christian Orthodox Church and Pühtitsa Convent face a Dec. 28 deadline to comply with a law restricting ties to foreign religious bodies deemed a security threat, or face dissolution. Estonian law restricts administrative ties to Moscow, although it allows religious ties. The church has challenged the law at the European Court of Human Rights.
Why have Russian and Estonian relations broken down?
Relations between Russia and Estonia have been strained for years, and they further deteriorated after Russia invaded Ukraine.
Although Soviet Russia recognized Estonia as an independent state in 1920, Moscow has long sought to exert influence over its neighbor. The Soviet Union annexed Estonia in 1940 during World War II, before Nazi Germany occupied the Baltic state from 1941 to 1944. Soviet forces retook Estonia and placed it under Moscow’s rule until 1991, when Estonia regained its independence. The same year, the two countries restored diplomatic relations, and Russia began a phased withdrawal of its troops.
In 2004, Estonia joined both NATO and the E.U. Its border with Russia thus became part of the E.U.’s external border. A decade later, Estonia and Russia signed treaties defining their land border and maritime boundaries, but the treaties were never ratified.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine triggered a breakdown in diplomatic ties. Estonia closed Russia’s consular offices in Narva and Tartu in 2022. In January 2023, the two countries expelled their ambassadors and downgraded bilateral representation to charges d’affaires.
Tensions have continued to escalate as the war has dragged on. In September 2025, NATO said three Russian fighter jets entered Estonian airspace. Earlier this year, Estonia began introducing overnight closures at certain road checkpoints, citing border incidents from the Russian side.
In recent weeks, Russia has escalated pressure on other countries bordering Ukraine. Last week, two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed on Poland during a major Russian attack on Ukraine. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared to be a deliberate provocation coinciding with European military drills in Poland. Days earlier, Moldova detected seven drones in its airspace amid Russian strikes on Ukraine, prompting it to summon Moscow’s ambassador-designate.
Estonian authorities said Russia’s military intelligence agency ordered an attempted arson on Estonian drone maker Threod Systems on Nov. 14. Moscow denied involvement. “We do not warn about these threats without reason,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said about the foiled attack. Margo Palloson, Estonia’s domestic intelligence chief, told public broadcaster ERR that Russia has targeted around 10 Estonian defense companies.
In a Politico op-ed published Tuesday, Tsahkna said Estonia was closing its land border in response to “a growing number of acts of sabotage and intimidation” by Russia. He cited Polish authorities’ allegations that Russian intelligence services were behind an arson attack on Warsaw’s Marywilska shopping center, Germany’s discovery of an alleged Russian explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport, and Denmark’s claim that it foiled an alleged Russian intelligence plot to kill an American-Ukrainian citizen.
“These incidents form part of a broader Russian campaign targeting the whole of Europe, including countries far beyond its borders. The aim is to undermine the European security order, intimidate its neighbors and dictate the choices of sovereign nations,” Tsahkna wrote. “Closing our border will not eliminate these threats, but it will limit opportunities for hostile intelligence activities. It will also help close channels for sanctions evasion, a crucial part of depriving Russia of the resources it uses to finance its war economy and sustain its aggression.”
Whether the latest dispute will lead to open conflict is uncertain. Jennifer Kavanagh and Jeremy Shapiro argued in a December 2025 European Council on Foreign Relations report that a limited, deniable operation designed to test NATO’s unity was more likely than a direct Russian invasion of Estonia. An armed attack by Russia on Estonia could trigger NATO’s collective defense obligations, raising the risk of a wider war in Europe. Rutte reassured in October that there was “no imminent threat against NATO territory.”
Leonard Schütte, an expert on transatlantic security, wrote in May for the German Marshall Fund , however, that doubts about U.S. commitment to Europe could make Moscow more willing to test NATO in the next few years. In September, Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem said Russia could be in a position to use military force against Estonia within a year if fighting in Ukraine ended within six months.
“Russia could use a military force of size ‘X’ against us. Are our preparations matching that? Are we capable of eliminating a military force of that size? And if we are not, then we should make those necessary preparations?” Herem said. “Or there is another option: We can all sign off on keeping our fingers crossed that it will not happen and do nothing at all.”
